translation_en: Harun ibn Sa‘id al-Ayli narrated to us: Abdullah ibn Wahb narrated to us: Sulayman—Ibn Bilal—informed me: Yahya informed me: Ubayd ibn Hunayn informed me that he heard Abdullah ibn Abbas narrate: Umar ibn al-Khattab narrated to me, who said: I spent a year wanting to ask Umar about a verse, but I could not bring myself to do so until he went out for pilgrimage. I went with him. On the return journey, he turned aside toward the arak trees to attend to a need. I waited for him until he finished, then walked with him and said, “Commander of the Faithful, who were the two wives of the Messenger of Allah who joined together against him?” He said, “They were Hafsah and Aishah.” I said, “By Allah, I have wanted to ask you about this for a year, but I could not out of awe of you.” He said, “Do not do that. Whatever you think I know, ask me about it; if I know it, I will tell you.” Umar said: By Allah, in the pre-Islamic days we did not consider women to have any say, until Allah revealed what He revealed about them and allotted to them what He allotted. While I was considering a matter and discussing it, my wife said to me, “If you did such-and-such…” I said to her, “What business is it of yours? Why are you involving yourself in what I intend to do?” She said, “How strange you are, son of al-Khattab! You do not want anyone to answer you back, while your daughter answers back to the Messenger of Allah until he remains angry all day.” Umar said: I took my cloak and went straight to Hafsah. I said, “My daughter, do you answer back to the Messenger of Allah until he remains angry all day?” Hafsah said, “By Allah, we do answer him back.” I said, “You know that I am warning you against Allah’s punishment and the Messenger’s anger. My daughter, do not be deceived by this woman whose beauty and the Messenger of Allah’s love for her have impressed her”—meaning Aishah. Then I went to Umm Salamah, to whom I was related, and spoke to her. Umm Salamah said to me, “How strange you are, son of al-Khattab! You have intervened in everything, and now you want to intervene between the Messenger of Allah and his wives?” Her words struck me so sharply that they restrained some of what I had felt, and I left her. I had an Ansari companion: when I was away he brought me news, and when he was away I brought him news. At that time we feared a king of the Ghassanids; it had been reported to us that he intended to march against us, and our hearts were full of fear of him. My Ansari companion came and knocked at the door, saying, “Open, open!” I said, “Has the Ghassanid come?” He said, “Something more serious than that: the Messenger of Allah has stayed apart from his wives.” I said, “May Hafsah and Aishah be disgraced!” I took my clothes and went out until I reached the Messenger of Allah. He was in an upper chamber that could be reached by a ladder, and a black servant of the Messenger of Allah was at the top of the steps. I said, “This is Umar.” I was given permission. Umar said: I told the Messenger of Allah this whole story. When I reached what Umm Salamah had said, the Messenger of Allah smiled. He was lying on a mat with nothing between him and it. Beneath his head was a leather pillow stuffed with palm fiber. Near his feet were some acacia pods heaped together, and by his head were some hides hanging up. I saw the marks of the mat on the Messenger of Allah’s side and wept. He said, “Why are you weeping?” I said, “Messenger of Allah, Chosroes and Caesar live as they do, while you are the Messenger of Allah.” The Messenger of Allah said, “Are you not pleased that they have this world and you have the Hereafter?”
